r1.text: The Buddha went on his way, modestly and deep in his thoughts, his calm face was neither happy nor sad, it seemed to smile quietly and inwardly. With a hidden smile, quiet, calm, somewhat resembling a healthy child, the Buddha walked, wore the robe and placed his feet just as all of his monks did, according to a precise rule. But his face and his walk, his quietly lowered glance, his quietly dangling hand and even every finger of his quietly dangling hand expressed peace, expressed perfection, did not search, did not imitate, breathed softly in an unwithering calm, in an unwithering light, an untouchable peace.

r2.text: Siddhartha did not answer. He felt little curiosity for the teachings, he did not believe that they would teach him anything new, but he had, just as Govinda had, heard the contents of this Buddha's teachings again and again, though these reports only represented second- or third-hand information. But attentively he looked at Gotama's head, his shoulders, his feet, his quietly dangling hand, and it seemed to him as if every joint of every finger of this hand was of these teachings, spoke of, breathed of, exhaled the fragrant of, glistened of truth. This man, this Buddha was truthful down to the gesture of his last finger. This man was holy. Never before had Siddhartha venerated a person so much, never before had he loved a person as much as this one.

r3.text: But in the evening, when the heat cooled down and everyone in the camp started to bustle about and gathered around, they heard the Buddha teaching. They heard his voice, and it was also perfected, was of perfect calmness, was full of peace. Gotama taught the teachings of suffering, of the origin of suffering, of the way to relieve suffering. Calmly and clearly his quiet speech flowed on. Suffering was life, full of suffering was the world, but salvation from suffering had been found: salvation was obtained by him who would walk the path of the Buddha. With a soft, yet firm voice the exalted one spoke, taught the four main doctrines, taught the eightfold path, patiently he went the usual path of the teachings, of the examples, of the repetitions, brightly and quietly his voice hovered over the listeners, like a light, like a starry sky.

r4.text: Siddhartha awakened as if he had been asleep, when he heard Govinda's words. For a long time, he looked into Govinda's face. Then he spoke quietly, in a voice without mockery: "Govinda, my friend, now you have taken this step, now you have chosen this path. Always, O Govinda, you've been my friend, you've always walked one step behind me. Often I have thought: Won't Govinda for once also take a step by himself, without me, out of his own soul? Behold, now you've turned into a man and are choosing your path for yourself. I wish that you would go it up to its end, O my friend, that you shall find salvation!"

r5.text: Quietly, Gotama had listened to him, unmoved. Now he spoke, the perfected one, with his kind, with his polite and clear voice: "You've heard the teachings, O son of a Brahmin, and good for you that you've thought about it thus deeply. You've found a gap in it, an error. You should think about this further. But be warned, O seeker of knowledge, of the thicket of opinions and of arguing about words. There is nothing to opinions, they may be beautiful or ugly, smart or foolish, everyone can support them or discard them. But the teachings, you've heard from me, are no opinion, and their goal is not to explain the world to those who seek knowledge. They have a different goal; their goal is salvation from suffering. This is what Gotama teaches, nothing else."

r6.text: It is not my place to judge another person's life. Only for myself, for myself alone, I must decide, I must choose, I must refuse. Salvation from the self is what we Samanas search for, O exalted one. If I merely were one of your disciples, O venerable one, I'd fear that it might happen to me that only seemingly, only deceptively my self would be calm and be redeemed, but that in truth it would live on and grow, for then I had replaced my self with the teachings, my duty to follow you, my love for you, and the community of the monks!"

r7.text: I have never before seen a person glance and smile, sit and walk this way, he thought; truly, I wish to be able to glance and smile, sit and walk this way, too, thus free, thus venerable, thus concealed, thus open, thus childlike and mysterious. Truly, only a person who has succeeded in reaching the innermost part of his self would glance and walk this way. Well so, I also will seek to reach the innermost part of my self.

r8.text: At sunrise, they saw with astonishment what a large crowd of believers and curious people had spent the night here. On all paths of the marvellous grove, monks walked in yellow robes, under the trees they sat here and there, in deep contemplation—or in a conversation about spiritual matters, the shady gardens looked like a city, full of people, bustling like bees. The majority of the monks went out with their alms-dish, to collect food in town for their lunch, the only meal of the day. The Buddha himself, the enlightened one, was also in the habit of taking this walk to beg in the morning.

r9.text: I am deprived by the Buddha, thought Siddhartha, I am deprived, and even more he has given to me. He has deprived me of my friend, the one who had believed in me and now believes in him, who had been my shadow and is now Gotama's shadow. But he has given me Siddhartha, myself.

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: The Buddha dresses far more richly than the monks around him.
Every part of the Buddha's bearing expresses perfect peace.
The Buddha hurries through town, seeking the most generous alms.
The Buddha looks sad and weary after his long journey.
A.explanation: The passage says his face, walk, glance and "every finger" "expressed peace, expressed perfection," which is its main point. He walks "modestly" and "did not search," so eager searching is wrong. He wears the robe "just as all of his monks did," not more richly. His face is "neither happy nor sad," not tired.

A.prompt: According to the passage, why did most of the monks go out with their alms-dish?
options: To carry water from the river back to the grove
To give away food to the poor families in town
To invite new pilgrims into the grove to hear the teachings
To collect food in town for their only meal of the day
A.explanation: The passage says the monks "went out with their alms-dish, to collect food in town for their lunch, the only meal of the day." Giving away food reverses this; they collect it. Carrying water is not mentioned. Inviting pilgrims is not why they go out; the crowd had already gathered on its own.

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "modestly" most nearly means
options: shyly
secretly
slowly
humbly
A.explanation: The Buddha walks "modestly and deep in his thoughts," wearing the same robe as his monks and seeking no attention, so "humbly" fits. "Shyly" adds a nervousness the calm passage denies. "Slowly" concerns speed, which the word does not describe. "Secretly" is wrong; he walks openly through the town.

options: does not intend to follow Govinda onto this path
has already decided to join the Buddha's community together with Govinda at sunrise
is angry that Govinda acted without asking him
wants Govinda to return with him to the Samanas
A.explanation: He wishes that Govinda "would go it up to its end," speaking of "your path," which implies he will not take it himself. Joining together contradicts that. He praises Govinda for choosing "for yourself," so he is not angry. Returning to the Samanas is never proposed.

A.prompt: Based on the passage, what does Siddhartha feel he has gained from the Buddha?
options: His friend Govinda, as a lifelong follower
The Buddha's teachings
A place among the monks
Himself
A.explanation: He says, "he has given me Siddhartha, myself," so he has gained himself. He has lost Govinda, who "is now Gotama's shadow," so gaining his friend is wrong. He has not accepted the teachings. He has not joined the monks, so he has no place among them.

A.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "He has deprived me of my friend"
"I am deprived by the Buddha, thought Siddhartha"
"But he has given me Siddhartha, myself."
"who had been my shadow and is now Gotama's shadow"
A.explanation: Only "he has given me Siddhartha, myself" names what he gained. The line about being deprived of his friend names a loss. "I am deprived by the Buddha" also states a loss. "Who had been my shadow" describes Govinda's change, not what Siddhartha gained.

A.prompt: The sentence beginning "Suffering was life" mainly serves to
options: move from the problem of suffering to its promised solution
list the names of the Buddha's many disciples
show that the listeners disagreed with what Gotama said
describe the cooling evening weather in the grove
A.explanation: It states the problem ("Suffering was life") then turns with "but salvation from suffering had been found," moving to the solution. The weather is mentioned earlier, not in this sentence. No disciples are named. The listeners are not shown disagreeing; the voice hovers over them "like a light."

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha is eager to learn the teachings, hoping they hold something new.
Siddhartha feels jealous of Govinda's growing love for the Buddha.
Though not curious about the teachings, Siddhartha deeply reveres the Buddha himself.
Siddhartha thinks the Buddha is just an ordinary wandering monk.
A.explanation: He "felt little curiosity for the teachings," yet "never before had Siddhartha venerated a person so much," which the key combines. He did not believe they "would teach him anything new," so eagerness is wrong. He calls the Buddha "holy," not ordinary. Jealousy toward Govinda is not mentioned.

A.prompt: According to the passage, what is the goal of Gotama's teachings?
options: To explain the whole world
Salvation from suffering
To gather many disciples
To win arguments about words
A.explanation: Gotama says "their goal is salvation from suffering." He says the teachings' goal "is not to explain the world to those who seek knowledge," so explaining the world to lovers of argument is wrong. He warns against "arguing about words." Gathering disciples is never named as the goal.

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "astonishment" most nearly means
options: anger
fear
amazement
boredom
A.explanation: They see "with astonishment what a large crowd" had spent the night there, so the sense is amazement. "Fear" suggests danger, but the crowd is peaceful. Boredom does not fit a surprising sight. Anger is not suggested; nothing upsets them.

A.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha fears that becoming a disciple would
options: force him to leave his friend Govinda behind
only seem to free him from his self
make the monks angry enough to drive him away
require him to give up eating and sleeping
A.explanation: He fears that "only seemingly, only deceptively my self would be calm," while it would "live on and grow," so it would only seem to free him. Angry monks are not mentioned. Becoming a disciple would join him to Govinda, not separate them. Eating is not discussed.

A.prompt: The phrase "bustling like bees" suggests that the gardens were
options: crowded and full of busy movement
quiet and nearly empty
covered with bright flowers
dangerous, as if crowds might sting
A.explanation: The gardens "looked like a city, full of people," and the bee comparison adds busy movement. The danger of stinging is not the point; the crowd is peaceful. "Quiet and nearly empty" is the opposite of "full of people." Flowers are not mentioned; the image concerns activity, not plants.

B.prompt: According to the passage, which of the following did Gotama teach?
options: The art of fasting, as the Samanas taught
The verses of the Rig-Veda
The way to walk on water
The eightfold path
B.explanation: The passage says he "taught the four main doctrines, taught the eightfold path." Holding the breath and fasting are Samana exercises from the previous chapter. The Rig-Veda belongs to the Brahmins' teaching. Walking on water is something Govinda jokes about earlier, not Gotama's teaching.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "unmoved" most nearly means
options: motionless
undisturbed
unconvinced
unkind
B.explanation: Gotama listens "quietly" and answers kindly, so "unmoved" means undisturbed. "Motionless" takes the physical sense too far. "Unconvinced" is a possible meaning, but he praises Siddhartha's thinking, so his calm, not disagreement, is stressed. He speaks "with his kind" voice, so "unkind" is wrong.

B.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha's reverence for the Buddha comes mainly from
options: many second-hand reports he heard of the teachings
Govinda's eager and constant praise of the teachings
the size of the crowd that follows him
the way the man himself looks and moves
B.explanation: He looks at Gotama's "head, his shoulders, his feet, his quietly dangling hand," and finds truth there, so his reverence comes from the man himself. The second-hand reports did not stir his curiosity. The crowd is not mentioned here. Govinda's praise is not given as the source.

B.prompt: Based on the passage, what does Siddhartha resolve to do?
options: Go back home to his father's house
Seek the innermost part of his own self
Find another teacher, better than the Buddha
Return and ask the Buddha to accept him after all
B.explanation: He concludes, "I also will seek to reach the innermost part of my self." Becoming a disciple is not what he resolves; he looks to his own self. Finding a better teacher is not mentioned; he turns inward instead. His father's house is not mentioned here.

B.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "I have never before seen a person glance and smile, sit and walk this way, he thought"
"truly, I wish to be able to glance and smile, sit and walk this way, too"
"Truly, only a person who has succeeded in reaching the innermost part of his self would glance and walk this way."
"Well so, I also will seek to reach the innermost part of my self."
B.explanation: Only "I also will seek to reach the innermost part of my self" states his resolution. "Never before seen" records his amazement. "I wish to be able to glance and smile" states a wish, not a decision. The "only a person who has succeeded" line explains the Buddha's bearing rather than stating what Siddhartha will do.

B.prompt: Siddhartha's remark that Govinda had "always walked one step behind" him mainly serves to
options: criticize Govinda for choosing to follow the Buddha
show that Govinda walks more slowly because he is tired
set up a contrast with Govinda now choosing a path by himself
explain why the two friends had left the Samanas
B.explanation: He recalls Govinda always following, then says "now you've turned into a man and are choosing your path for yourself," a contrast. Physical speed is not the point. He praises rather than criticizes Govinda's choice. Leaving the Samanas is not explained here.

B.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha must choose his own path and does not judge others who follow the teachings.
Siddhartha believes that all of the Buddha's monks should leave the community and return to the world.
Siddhartha thinks the teachings are false.
Siddhartha wants to become the leader of the monks.
B.explanation: He says "It is not my place to judge another person's life. Only for myself... I must decide." He calls their lives not his to judge, so the claim that all monks should leave reverses him. He does not seek leadership. He never calls the teachings false; his concern is what discipleship would do to his self.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "concealed" most nearly means
options: hidden
punished
proud
tired
B.explanation: Siddhartha admires a manner "thus venerable, thus concealed, thus open, thus childlike and mysterious," pairing concealed with open and mysterious, so it means hidden. Punishment has nothing to do with the list. "Tired" contradicts the free, venerable bearing he admires. "Proud" does not fit a manner he calls childlike.

B.prompt: The phrases "did not search, did not imitate" mainly serve to
options: show that the Buddha has lost his way in the town
suggest that the Buddha copies his own monks
stress that the Buddha shows no striving or effort
contrast the Buddha with the woman who gave food
B.explanation: Set beside "breathed softly in an unwithering calm," the phrases show an absence of striving. Being lost is not suggested; he walks "according to a precise rule." "Did not imitate" denies copying. The woman who gave food does not appear in this passage.

B.prompt: Gotama's reply suggests that Siddhartha's objection
options: proves the teachings are full of errors
mistakes the purpose of the teachings
is the first time anyone has questioned him
has made Gotama angry with him
B.explanation: Gotama says the teachings "are no opinion" and their goal "is not to explain the world," implying the objection mistakes their purpose. He says Siddhartha should "think about this further," not throw anything away. He speaks kindly, so he is not angry. Nothing says this is the first question he has faced.

B.prompt: The passage is presented mainly as
options: a speech Siddhartha gives to the crowd of monks
Govinda's report to the other monks in the grove
Siddhartha's private thoughts after the Buddha turns away
a description of the grove by the narrator
B.explanation: The passage uses "I" and "he thought," so it presents Siddhartha's private thoughts. He speaks to no crowd. Govinda has left with the novices and does not report anything. The grove is not described; the passage records reflection about the Buddha's glance and smile.

B.prompt: How does Passage 2 reflect on the change shown in Passage 1?
options: It counts Govinda's choice as a loss but also as a gift of selfhood.
It shows Siddhartha regretting his good wish for Govinda.
It shows that Siddhartha has persuaded Govinda to leave the Buddha and walk with him once again.
It describes Govinda's first day as a monk.
B.explanation: In Passage 1 Govinda chooses his own path; in Passage 2 Siddhartha says he is "deprived" of his friend yet "given... myself." Govinda does not leave the Buddha. His first day as a monk is not described. Siddhartha does not regret his wish; he reflects on what he has gained.

C.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: Gotama admits his teaching is only one opinion, no better than the young man's own view.
Gotama explains the causes of every event in the world.
Gotama sternly orders Siddhartha to leave the grove at once.
Gotama separates his teaching, aimed at salvation, from mere opinions about the world.
C.explanation: Gotama says the teachings "are no opinion" and their goal is "salvation from suffering," separating them from opinions. He denies they are opinion, so the choice calling his teaching one opinion among many is wrong. He speaks politely and orders nothing. He says explaining the world is not their goal.

C.prompt: The passage suggests that Gotama's way of teaching was meant to
options: reach many listeners through patience and repetition
test which of the pilgrims were clever enough to join his monks
confuse listeners so they would depend on him
entertain the tired crowd after a hot day
C.explanation: He "patiently... went the usual path of the teachings, of the examples, of the repetitions," which suggests a method for reaching many listeners. His speech is "calmly and clearly" given, not confusing. No test of cleverness is described. The teaching concerns suffering, not entertainment.

C.prompt: The final sentence of the passage mainly serves to
options: show that Siddhartha has changed his mind about joining
explain why becoming a disciple would defeat Siddhartha's own aim
list the many daily duties that the monks must perform in the grove
praise the community of the monks and its rules
C.explanation: He fears he would have "replaced my self with the teachings," so his self would survive, defeating his aim of salvation from the self. The items named are not a list of daily duties. The sentence warns rather than praises. He has not changed his mind; he still refuses.

C.prompt: What does the passage suggest made Siddhartha revere the Buddha?
options: The size and wealth of the grove
The praise of the woman in Savathi
The new and surprising ideas he heard in the teachings
The truthfulness shown in the man's every gesture
C.explanation: He sees truth in "every joint of every finger" and calls the Buddha "truthful down to the gesture of his last finger." He expects nothing new from the teachings. The grove's size and wealth are not mentioned here. The woman's words are in an earlier scene and are not his reason.

C.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "This man, this Buddha was truthful down to the gesture of his last finger."
"Never before had Siddhartha venerated a person so much"
"though these reports only represented second- or third-hand information"
"He felt little curiosity for the teachings, he did not believe that they would teach him anything new"
C.explanation: Only "truthful down to the gesture of his last finger" ties his reverence to the man's gestures. The line about little curiosity explains what did not move him. "Never before had Siddhartha venerated" shows how much he revered, not why. The line on second-hand reports concerns the teachings, not the man.

C.prompt: As used in the passage, "deceptively" most nearly means
options: quickly
cleverly
falsely
gently
C.explanation: He fears his self would be calm "only seemingly, only deceptively," while in truth it lives on, so the sense is falsely. "Cleverly" suggests admiration, not falseness. "Gently" and "quickly" describe manner and speed, which the passage does not discuss.

C.prompt: The comparison "like a light, like a starry sky" mainly suggests that Gotama's voice
options: could only be heard by listeners after dark
was so loud and harsh it hurt the listeners' ears
seemed calm, bright and far-reaching to his listeners
frightened the listeners sitting nearest him
C.explanation: His voice "brightly and quietly... hovered over the listeners," so the images suggest calm, bright reach. "Loud and harsh" contradicts "soft, yet firm." The time of night is real but the simile describes quality, not when it could be heard. Light and stars suggest comfort, not fear.

C.prompt: Siddhartha's thoughts imply that such a glance and walk come from
options: living among the crowds of a busy grove
studying many teachers' doctrines for many years
being born into a Brahmin family
reaching the innermost part of one's self
C.explanation: He thinks "only a person who has succeeded in reaching the innermost part of his self would glance and walk this way." Studying many teachers is what he now rejects. The crowded grove is not the cause. Birth as a Brahmin is not mentioned.

C.prompt: The repetition in "I am deprived, and even more he has given to me" mainly serves to
options: present Siddhartha's loss and gain as a paradox
stress how much the Buddha owns and gives away
show Siddhartha demanding that Govinda be returned
show that Siddhartha has already forgotten Govinda
C.explanation: The repeated "deprived" is answered by "even more he has given," pairing loss and gain. He speaks only in thought, so he demands nothing. He names Govinda, so he has not forgotten him. Ownership is not meant; what was "given" is Siddhartha himself.

C.prompt: The narrator's description of the Buddha is best described as
options: amused and slightly mocking of the monks
admiring and attentive to the smallest details
hurried, vague and uninterested in detail
critical, pointing out faults in how the Buddha walks
C.explanation: The narrator notes even "every finger of his quietly dangling hand," praising peace and perfection, so the description is admiring and detailed. No faults are named. Nothing mocks him. Close attention to fingers and glance is the opposite of hurried and vague.

C.prompt: How does Siddhartha's statement in Passage 2 relate to Gotama's claim in Passage 1?
options: He accuses Gotama of lying to his listeners about salvation.
He rejects salvation and says the world should be explained by opinions.
He accepts salvation as the goal but argues that teachings would defeat it for him.
He agrees to become a disciple of Gotama after all.
C.explanation: Gotama names "salvation from suffering"; Siddhartha says "salvation from the self is what we Samanas search for" but fears teachings would only "seemingly" free him. He seeks salvation, so the choice saying he rejects salvation is wrong. He refuses discipleship. He never accuses Gotama of lying.

C.prompt: How does Passage 2 build on the admiration shown in Passage 1?
options: It shows Siddhartha becoming one of the monks in the grove.
It turns admiration for the Buddha into a resolution about his own path.
It describes Siddhartha meeting a second holy man on the road.
It shows Siddhartha deciding the Buddha was not truly holy.
C.explanation: Passage 1 shows reverence; in Passage 2 he wishes to walk "this way, too" and resolves to "seek to reach the innermost part of my self." He still calls him holy. No second holy man appears. He refuses to join the monks.
